title: Paul Stands Firm on Who Belongs
overview: Paul recounts how the early church's leaders accepted his message to non-Jews, and how he later confronted Peter for pulling away from non-Jewish believers at meals.

parts.label: Return to Jerusalem (vv. 1-5)
parts.note: Paul went back to Jerusalem with Barnabas and Titus, a non-Jewish believer, and privately laid out his message before the church's leaders. When some people Paul calls false believers pushed for Titus to be circumcised, the rite marking Jewish men under the law of Moses, Paul refused, since giving in would make it look required of every non-Jew.

parts.label: The leaders shake hands (vv. 6-10)
parts.note: James, Peter (called Cephas, his Aramaic name) and John added nothing to Paul's message and accepted him as a partner, agreeing that Paul would focus on non-Jews and Peter on Jews. Their only request was that Paul keep helping the poor, likely the struggling believers in Jerusalem.

parts.label: Clash at Antioch (vv. 11-14)
parts.note: Peter had been eating with non-Jewish believers but pulled back when visitors linked to James arrived, and other Jewish believers, even Barnabas, followed him. Sharing a table signaled full acceptance, so Paul publicly challenged Peter for implying non-Jews had to adopt Jewish customs to belong.

parts.label: Made right through trust (vv. 15-16)
parts.note: Paul starts from a common Jewish view of the time, which counted non-Jews as sinners because they lived outside the law. He then says that even those born Jewish know a person is made right with God by trusting Christ, not by keeping the law of Moses.

parts.label: Living a new life (vv. 17-21)
parts.note: Paul says that setting aside the law's rules to trust Christ does not make Christ a promoter of sin, and that going back to those rules would be the real failure. He pictures his old self as having died with Christ on the cross, so he now lives by trust in Jesus, and if the law could make people right, Christ's death would have been pointless.

disagreement: Christians differ over what "works of the law" means here: many read it as any human effort to earn God's approval, while others read it mainly as Jewish identity markers like circumcision and food laws that were being used to keep non-Jews out.
think: Have you ever gone along with a group's unspoken rules about who belongs, even when you disagreed, and what made that hard to resist?
